newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke seen leaving rates on hold Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke seen leaving rates on hold Wednesday.

text.p: Continuing signs of low inflation mean British finance minister Kenneth Clarke can safely obey his political instincts and leave interest rates at six percent at Wednesday's monetary meeting, analysts said on Monday.
"I wouldn't say the Chancellor's first thoughts weren't politics but he can certainly make an economic case for leaving rates unchanged," NatWest Markets UK economist Geoff Dicks said.
The narrow money supply measure M0 grew a seasonally adjusted 6.5 percent from a year earlier, down sharply from 7.3 percent in January, the Bank of England said on Monday.
Moreover, a monthly survey showed the index for prices paid by purchasing managers falling to 39.7 in February from 41.2 in January, the largest drop since July 1996.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke refused a Bank of England request in January to raise interest rates, arguing that there were signs demand was already weakening.
But aside from the economic case for leaving rates on hold, analysts say Clarke would not want to antagonize voters by increasing the cost of borrowing now despite Bank of England requests.

"The proximity of the general election and the monumental task the Conservative party faces to stand any change of winning, means that the Chancellor will be wearing earplugs," UBS economist Andrew Cates said.
The Conservative Party is widely expected to hold a general election on May 1 but is 20 points behind the opposition Labour party in opinion polls.

Clarke is expected to use a speech to the British Retail Consortium this evening to rule out a pre-election rate rise. But analysts say this will not stop Bank of England Governor Eddie George from pressing again for a 25 basis point rate rise to deliver 2.5 percent or lower inflation in the medium term.
However a Reuter survey of 20 economists showed the governor is likely to be overruled. None expected rates to be unmoved after Wednesday's meeting.

"The view has to be that there is no possibility of a pre-election rate rise," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd. He added that Monday's data bolstered Clarke's position that rates do not need to go up. The strength of sterling is another key factor in Clarke's favour and is helping to keep inflation pressures in check.
CIBC chief economist David Coleman says the disagreement between Clarke and George is actually over the role of the pound rather than over a mere 25 basis points on interest rates.
"Mr Clarke is right to say we shouldn't dismiss the exchange rate as a one-off. It's no longer valid to argue that it's temporary, given it's been going up since August," he said.
"The exchange rate strength in sterling will have a dampening effect on the UK economy and therefore on inflation."
But after the election interest rates are expected to go up, whichever party wins.

"The rise might be slightly sharper under a Labour government because it can argue it's the fault of the mistakes of the previous government. They can win market credibility by being tough on inflation," Yamaichi's Shepperd said.
He suggested the re-elected Conservatives would opt for a single 25 basis point rise whilst Labour would probably go for two 25 basis point increases.
"It's not a crisis, which is the way one big move would be interpreted. Two quarter-point rises would give a better impression of controlled adjustment," he said.

CIBC's Coleman argues that a swift 25 basis point rate increase soon after the election would be a good way to improve credibility in financial markets and might prevent the need for more moves later.
"It's much cheaper to do it straight after the election than waiting until later in the year when inflation pressures are building," he said.

But Natwest Markets' Dicks argues that adjusting fiscal policy would be a much better way of cooling demand than raising interest rates. He suggests that if Labour wins, it should raise taxes in the budget it plans soon after taking office.
"That would be my preferred option -- indicate rates are capped at six percent and get sterling off these toppy levels," he said.
Labour has said it wil not increase income tax but has not ruled out other adjustments to the tax system.
